Q: How to make C shell exit immediately on Ctrl+D (EOF) when the buffer contains text? A:

There is some misunderstanding regarding the behavior of the terminal for Ctrl-D in cooked mode (the default mode where the terminal handles the backspace key).

  • when Ctrl-D is pressed by the user with pending input, the terminal returns to the caller of the read syscall with a non-zero length (the number of bytes read so far, copied to the destination buffer).

  • when Ctrl-D is pressed by the user with no pending input, the terminal returns to the caller of the read syscall with a length of 0 which means end-of-file.

You request input with fgets() from the stdin stream, presumably configured with the default setting, ie: line buffered when attached to a terminal. Note that both the terminal and the standard stream perform line buffering, but in the regular case, the newline character that causes the terminal to return to the caller also causes fgets() to return.

  • if the user types Ctrl-D in the middle of a line, the terminal echoes ^D and returns the number of bytes typed so far and fgets() receives them and stores them to the destination array, space permitting. Since none of these bytes is a newline ('\n') fgets() keeps requesting more bytes from the stream and the terminal is requested again. Nothing happens until the user presses another Ctrl-D or a newline...

  • If indeed the user presses a second Ctrl-D in a row, the terminal will return 0 and the stream will consider that an end-of-file, setting the end-of-file indicator and fgets() will return the line that does not end with a newline. feof() will return non zero after fgets() returns and you should get the expected behavior.

  • If instead the user presses a the Enter key, the newline is read and the terminal returns to the caller (the stream library) and fgets() returns the full line "ls\n", the end-of-file indicator is not set and the command is executed as if the initial Ctrl-D had not been typed.

To perform something special upon Ctrl-D, you need to set the terminal to raw mode and handle line editing yourself, assigning the special semantics to Ctrl-D as to other special keys. This is typically what the shells do.

Q: How do I configure Qt for cross-compilation from Linux to Windows target? A:

Another way to cross-compile software for Windows on Linux is the MinGW-w64 toolchain on Archlinux. It is easy to use and maintain, and it provides recent versions of the compiler and many libraries. I personally find it easier than MXE and it seems to adopt newer versions of libraries faster.

First, you will need an arch-based machine (virtual machine or docker container will suffice). It does not have to be Arch Linux, derivatives will do as well. I used Manjaro Linux. Most of the MinGW-w64 packages are not available at the official Arch repositories, but there is plenty in AUR. The default package manager for Arch (Pacman) does not support installation directly from AUR, so you will need to install and use an AUR wrapper like yay or yaourt. Then installing MinGW-w64 version of Qt5 and Boost libraries is as easy as:

yay -Sy mingw-w64-qt5-base mingw-w64-boost
#yaourt -Sy mingw-w64-qt5-base mingw-w64-qt5-boost #if you use yaourt

This will also install the MinGW-w64 toolchain (mingw-w64-gcc) and other dependencies. Cross-compiling a Qt project for windows (x64) is then as simple as:

x86_64-w64-mingw32-qmake-qt5
make

To deploy your program you will need to copy corresponding dlls from /usr/x86_64-w64-mingw32/bin/. For example, you will typically need to copy /usr/x86_64-w64-mingw32/lib/qt/plugins/platforms/qwindows.dll to program.exe_dir/platforms/qwindows.dll.

To get a 32bit version you simply need to use i686-w64-mingw32-qmake-qt5 instead. Cmake-based projects work just as easily with x86_64-w64-mingw32-cmake. This approach worked extremely well for me, was the easiest to set-up, maintain, and extend. It also goes well with continuous integration services. There are docker images available too.

For example, let's say I want to build QNapi subtitle downloader GUI. I could do it in two steps:

  1. Start the docker container:
sudo docker run -it burningdaylight/mingw-arch:qt /bin/bash
  1. Clone and compile QNapi
git clone --recursive 'https://github.com/QNapi/qnapi.git' 
cd qnapi/ 
x86_64-w64-mingw32-qmake-qt5
make

That's it! In many cases, it will be that easy. Adding your own libraries to the package repository (AUR) is also straightforward. You would need to write a PKBUILD file, which is as intuitive as it can get, see mingw-w64-rapidjson, for example.

Q: how to make my program be displayed only in tray and not in taskbar and hide the console window A:

You need to add #![windows_subsystem = "windows"] at the top of your main.rs file.

This will set the windows subsystem to WINDOWS instead of the default CONSOLE and make your program behave the way you want.

Q: CAShapeLayer and UIBezierPath artifacts on touch A:

I had the exact same issue using UIBezierPath

For some reason this solved the artifacts:

node.lineCap = .round
node.anchorPoint = CGPoint.zero

Q: What is in Angular the correct term of a public property in an object component that contains form data or display data? A:

The model is only the "json object".

We talk about "form-model" to reference to the "control". It's more easy understand when you use ReactiveForms or FormSignal: the "form-model" is the formGroup or the form signal (a complex object with properties of value, binding, valuesChange...

When use [ngModel] you create also a NgControl with these properties about value, binding valueChange..., (but it's some "transparent" because you use a directive in the .html). You can say that "item.name" it's not only a property of item, else a NgControl, or a "form-model" of this property.

So, item is only a model and it's not related to the server (can be,e.g. a variable)
